thread.title: Twilio : DOW JONES-Regaining Trust Is the No. 1 Issue for Tech in 2019

author: www.4-traders.com
title: Twilio : DOW JONES-Regaining Trust Is the No. 1 Issue for Tech in 2019
text:
As the tech industry looks back on a difficult 2018 and warily approaches the year to come, one word is increasingly on the lips of Silicon Valley executives: 'Trust is the No. 1 thing you sell,' Jeff Lawson
, chief executive of Twilio , told Barron's. With consumers, legislators, and investors more skeptical of tech than they've been in years, trust could well be an intangible factor next year in how companies compete, recruit new customers, and retain talent. A new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives could also change the regulatory equation in 2019.
'As corporate leaders, we have a responsibility to employees, customers, and society,' Twilio's (ticker: TWLO) Lawson said from the cloud-communications platform company's San Francisco headquarters this month. 'We're a company that determines who we do business with. If the Klan, for instance, tried to use our service to plan an event, we wouldn't allow it.'
Social-media companies spent most of 2018 trying to find a balance between free speech, safety, and running a sticky platform.
Facebook 's Mark Zuckerberg
initially defended users' right to deny the Holocaust before backtracking. And Apple (AAPL), Spotify Technology (SPOT), Facebook (FB), Twitter (TWTR), and Alphabet 's (GOOGL) YouTube all struggled with how to respond to hate-mongering from Alex Jones
and his InfoWars site. Most of these platforms eventually banned Jones, though Twitter decided to hold out for a while, putting the company in the unusual position of defending hate speech. Twilio notes that Jones was never a customer. Lawson reset Twilio's policy on hate speech after the violent white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va. , in August 2017 . Twilio does not allow any group whose mission or purpose is 'hateful' on its platform, regardless of their activity.
One could argue that Twilio's direct approach helped propel the stock 270% in 2018, even as the Nasdaq Composite fell 4.4%. Twilio's cloud platform is used by companies like Nordstrom (JWN) and U-Haul parent Amerco (UHAL) to engage digitally with costumers.
Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block
used the word 'trust' 18 times in a recent 45-minute interview. 'In our business model, everything starts with trust,' Block said. Salesforce.com (CRM) shares are up 32% in 2018. If there's a deficit of trust these days, Big Tech has itself to blame. Well before the market's late-year selloff, shares of Facebook and Twitter were pummeled for their roles in the 2016 presidential election, the spread of 'fake news,' and their perceived anticonservative bias. Google has also faced questions about its perceived anticonservative bias.
Earlier this year, Barron's argued that a new divide had emerged in tech, with ad-driven giants like Facebook and Google on one side and direct-to-consumer sales models like Apple and Netflix on the other. The ad-dependent, and thus data-driven, names were the ones struggling the most with trust.
Several of Silicon Valley's most-successful chief executives, led by Apple CEO Tim Cook
, were critical of how Facebook and Google share consumer data in an almost Faustian bargain with business partners and advertisers. Facebook shares, which peaked at $218.62 in late July, closed at $134.56 on Thursday-a drop of 38%. Twitter, which reached $47.79 in early July, closed at $28.68 on Thursday, down 40%. But even Apple has now been drawn into the privacy debate, in the case over its business dealings in China . And its stock has struggled mightily in the last quarter of the year.
Cook has insisted that Apple has not compromised user privacy in China , despite criticism that its decision to host Chinese users' iCloud accounts in a new data center within the country would give Chinese authorities easier access to text messages, email, and other data.
Investors, and Barron's, continue to debate the importance of trust when it comes to stock prices. In some cases, users have yet to show much concern. Facebook's still massive user base is one example-at last count, Facebook had 2.27 billion active monthly users.
But Silicon Valley executives have other worries, namely keeping talent. Employers are acutely aware that highly-skilled tech workers, already in great demand, have more leverage and feel unencumbered criticizing their bosses. Google employees took umbrage at the company's secret plan to build a censored search engine in China ( Google has no plans to relaunch the search engine, CEO Sundar Pichai
told a congressional panel on Tuesday, amid increased scrutiny of big tech firms). And Facebook lost the co-founders of Instagram and WhatsApp , which Facebook shelled out some $20 billion to buy, earlier this year. They were unhappy with Facebook 's direction and left money on the table to make their point. EDITORS' CHOICE

'We're in an era of the empowered tech employee,' Brian Halligan
, CEO and co-founder of HubSpot , an inbound marketing and sales software company, said over coffee in San Francisco's financial district recently. 'They expect more from their employers than financial compensation and the products they create. They want a place of good standing in society.' Mindful of what can happen to a high-profile public company that loses the trust of the public and its workforce, a batch of initial public-offering candidates have adopted greater due diligence, says David Larcker
, director of the Corporate Governance Research Initiative at Stanford's Graduate School of Business . If there's hope for change in 2019, it could come from those new public companies that have the chance to reset the notion of a 21st century tech company. Uber, Lyft , and Slack Technologies are reportedly finishing up their IPO paperwork. Their executives, lawyers, and investors would do well to put trust at their very top of their priority list.
